title: Saturday Mistakes Episode 1: 5 Common English Mistakes & How to Fix Them
dek: Five mistakes English learners often make, why they happen, and a simple pattern to fix each one. With examples and a mini-quiz for every mistake.

blocks.text: Welcome to **Saturday Mistakes**. Every week we look at five small mistakes that learners make, understand why they happen, and replace them with a pattern that sounds natural. Mistakes are not a problem. They are proof that you are learning.
blocks.say: Welcome to Saturday Mistakes. Every week we look at five small mistakes that learners make, understand why they happen, and replace them with a pattern that sounds natural. Mistakes are not a problem. They are proof that you are learning.

blocks.text: This week we look at five common mistakes in English. Every mistake follows the same steps: the sentence that is not quite right, the better sentence, the reason, a simple rule and a mini-quiz. **Notice the pattern, not just the individual sentence.**
blocks.say: This week we look at five common mistakes in English. Every mistake follows the same steps: the sentence that is not quite right, the better sentence, the reason, a simple rule and a mini-quiz. Notice the pattern, not just the individual sentence.

blocks.alt: Four steps: notice the mistake, understand why, learn the pattern, practise it. Mistakes are proof that you are learning.
blocks.caption: **The weekly routine.** Four small steps, every Saturday.

blocks.say: Future forms Spend time Double negatives Verbs + prepositions Preposition combinations

blocks.title: Future forms
blocks.wrong: “I will be go to the party tomorrow.”
blocks.right: “I will go to the party tomorrow.”
blocks.why: “Be” appears in many future sentences (“will be happy”, “will be working”), so learners add it everywhere.
blocks.rule: After **will**, use the base verb: will + go. Use **will be + verb-ing** only for an action in progress at a future time.
examples: I will be working at 9 a.m.

quiz.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: I will be visit my aunt.
quiz.explanation: After “will” we use the base verb: I will visit.

blocks.say: 1. Future forms. Not quite: “I will be go to the party tomorrow.”. Say this: “I will go to the party tomorrow.”. “Be” appears in many future sentences (“will be happy”, “will be working”), so learners add it everywhere. After will, use the base verb: will + go. Use will be + verb-ing only for an action in progress at a future time.

blocks.title: Spend time
blocks.why: Many languages use a word like “for” or “to” here, so learners translate it directly.
blocks.rule: Use **spend time + verb-ing**. Use “to + verb” to give a purpose: I study **to improve** my English.
examples: I spent an hour practising English.
I study to improve my English.

quiz.question: I spend 30 minutes ___ before bed.
quiz.explanation: “Spend time” is followed by the -ing form: reading.

blocks.say: 2. Spend time. Not quite: “I spent time for learning English.”. Say this: “I spent time learning English.”. Many languages use a word like “for” or “to” here, so learners translate it directly. Use spend time + verb-ing. Use “to + verb” to give a purpose: I study to improve my English.

blocks.title: Double negatives
blocks.right: “I don’t know anything about it.”  /  “I know nothing about it.”
blocks.why: In Spanish, Italian, French, Russian, Greek and many other languages, the negative is repeated (“no sé nada”). In standard English, one negative is enough.
blocks.rule: Choose **one** negative pattern: **no + noun** or **don’t/doesn’t + verb + any(thing)**.

quiz.question: I checked my bag, but…
quiz.explanation: With “don’t” we use “anything”. Or say it with one negative word: “I have nothing.”

blocks.say: 3. Double negatives. Not quite: “I don’t know nothing about it.”. Say this: “I don’t know anything about it.” / “I know nothing about it.”. In Spanish, Italian, French, Russian, Greek and many other languages, the negative is repeated (“no sé nada”). In standard English, one negative is enough. Choose one negative pattern: no + noun or don’t/doesn’t + verb + any(thing).

blocks.title: Verbs + prepositions
blocks.why: “Discuss” already means “talk about”, so “about” is extra. Other verbs need a small word: arrive **at**, listen **to**.
blocks.rule: Learn verbs with their pattern: **discuss** something, **listen to** something, **arrive at** the station.

quiz.question: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.explanation: “Discuss” has no preposition. “Listen” needs “to”: We listened to it.

blocks.say: 4. Verbs + prepositions. Not quite: “We discussed about the problem.”. Say this: “We discussed the problem.”. “Discuss” already means “talk about”, so “about” is extra. Other verbs need a small word: arrive at, listen to. Learn verbs with their pattern: discuss something, listen to something, arrive at the station.

blocks.title: Preposition combinations
blocks.why: Prepositions rarely translate word for word. The same idea uses different small words in different languages.
blocks.rule: Learn the whole expression: **depend on**, **interested in**, **good at**, **afraid of**, **wait for**.
blocks.say: 5. Preposition combinations. Not quite: “It depends of you.”. Say this: “It depends on you.”. Prepositions rarely translate word for word. The same idea uses different small words in different languages. Learn the whole expression: depend on, interested in, good at, afraid of, wait for.

items: Choose **two mistakes** that you sometimes make.
Write **three new sentences** for each one, using the rule.
Compare your sentences with the examples above.
Next week, listen for the same patterns in real conversations.
blocks.say: Choose two mistakes that you sometimes make. Write three new sentences for each one, using the rule. Say them aloud and record yourself. Compare your sentences with the examples above. Next week, listen for the same patterns in real conversations.

blocks.text: Notice the pattern. Practise the pattern. Make it your own. Which answer surprised you most? Write it down and use it in a sentence today.

blocks.text: The ideas in this article rest on published research and teaching practice. Start with any of these:

**Hattie, J., & Timperley, H. (2007).** The power of feedback. *Review of Educational Research, 77*(1), 81–112.
**James, C. (1998).** *Errors in Language Learning and Use: Exploring Error Analysis.* Longman.
**Lyster, R., & Ranta, L. (1997).** Corrective feedback and learner uptake: Negotiation of form in communicative classrooms. *Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 19*(1), 37–66.
**Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006).** Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. *Psychological Science, 17*(3), 249–255.
